en: Now, when we learned about functions, we
also learned about these levels of
abstraction, which in the end helped us
decide whether a function is doing too much.
It was a part of the decision process. For
classes, we also have a related helper
concept, you could say, which helps us
decide whether a class is too big or too
small in case you're not sure whether that
could be the case.
And that concept is called cohesion.
Now what's cohesion about?
Cohesion in the end just defines how well
the methods of a class are using the class
properties.
So how much are your class methods using the
properties of that class? That's what makes
up cohesion.
And you would have maximum cohesion inside
of a class if all
methods in the class, each would use all
class properties.
So every single method in a class uses all
the class properties.
If that's what you would have, then you
would have a highly cohesive object and you
would have maximum cohesion.
Now the opposite would be no cohesion.
That basically means that of all the methods
in your class, no method is using any class
property.
So all the class properties are not managed
by your methods. Instead, they probably are
public and can be used from outside the
class.
Then in the end, you would just have a data
structure, a container with some utility
methods as it seems since the methods are
not operating on the properties of the class
at all.
Now you definitely wanna avoid having a
class with no cohesion unless you wanna have
a data container utility methods. Otherwise,
you wanna avoid this.
The goal, of course, is
maximum cohesion,
though this is not entirely true. The goal
is high cohesion because you will never be
able or
rarely be able to achieve maximum cohesion.
Instead, you're going to be somewhere in
between and you wanna write highly cohesive
classes
where all your methods use many of your
properties.
You will not be able to make every method
use every property all the time, but you
should have a good usage of properties in
your methods.
For example, if you have a look at this
large class from before again, I added some
comment annotations next to the methods
about which properties these methods
probably would be using.
And I think it's fair to say that
addProduct, updateProduct, removeProduct,
getAvailableItems, and restockProduct
probably all
only operate on the offered products
property.
So they use one of the 3 properties you got.
createCustomer, loginCustomer,
these 2 methods probably only operate on
customers,
just as the updateCustomerProfile method, by
the way.
And then we only got makePurchase and
addOrder, which use all 3 properties
probably.
The orders, offered products, and customers
properties.
And refund would probably use customers and
orders.
So we can see that only makePurchase and
addOrder are methods that would really
belong into this kind of a class because
these are the methods which use all the
properties.
Refund at least uses 2 of the properties.
But generally, this class doesn't have a
great cohesion because almost all methods
use only one of the 3 properties.
So there is no hard rule
on when to split. You can't say if 7 out of
10 methods use at least 2 of 3 properties,
then that's good, otherwise you should
split. That's not how it works.
But it should be obvious that in this class,
many methods are only using 1 or at most 2
of the available properties. The majority
indeed only uses 1 property and that's not
cohesive at all.
Now, as soon as you start splitting your
classes into smaller classes, you should see
your cohesion grow. And definitely don't end
up with the one method per class solution
just because this has maximum cohesion.
As I mentioned on the slide, that's not the
goal. But you should end up with smaller
classes which have good cohesion. So where
most of your methods use at least a couple
of the available properties, that's the end
goal in the end.
